channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: Lucas Museum opens with comics, Star Wars and fine art under one roof
item.description: After 17 years of planning, George Lucas and Mellody Hobson's $1 billion Museum of Narrative Art is opening in Los Angeles. Its deliberately broad collection puts comic and popular art beside Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera and Banksy, with Star Wars models, a Naboo starfighter and even the dogs-playing-poker painting among the highlights.

item.title: A WooCommerce plugin flaw is under active attack
item.description: Attackers are exploiting an arbitrary file-upload flaw in the Wholesale Lead Capture Plugin for WooCommerce, which has more than 20,000 installations. The bug can permit unauthenticated PHP webshell uploads. Users should update to version 2.0.3.2 or later and inspect upload directories for unfamiliar PHP files.

item.title: An archaeologist argues for the value of messy digital fragments
item.description: William Caraher revisits “slow” and “punk” archaeology ahead of a conference on the digital, archaeological and ethical. His argument for fragments, ambiguity and incomplete records pushes back against tidy digital systems that can erase the uncertainty and human context that make historical evidence meaningful.

item.title: Public-domain classics keep becoming bargain-bin horror movies
item.description: A brisk, funny look at the wave of low-budget horror films built from expired copyrights, from Winnie-the-Pooh and Steamboat Willie to a zombie-flavored Wuthering Heights. It also inventories the next tempting targets, including Babar, Mrs Dalloway, The Sun Also Rises and The Age of Innocence.

item.title: Cory Doctorow makes the case for using an RSS reader
item.description: Doctorow argues that RSS is a rare personal choice that improves both your own internet experience and the wider web. Readers deliver posts without platform lock-in, tracking, pop-ups or algorithmic filtering, while supporting blogs, newsletters, Mastodon, Bluesky and other independent sources.

item.title: WordPress's plugin handbook is a practical map of extension development
item.description: The official Plugin Developer Handbook gathers the working details of WordPress extension development in one place: hooks, settings, metadata, REST endpoints, security, privacy, scheduled events, localization, directory submission and developer tools. It is a useful reference for both new plugins and old code that needs modernization.

item.title: A 1987 Atari newsletter binder becomes a computer-history time capsule
item.description: A surviving binder of 50 Atari user-group newsletters from August 1987 offers 700 pages of firsthand computing history: software rumors, CES discoveries, type-in code, online-service worries and the shift from 8-bit machines to the Atari ST. The Internet Archive has digitized the full collection.

item.title: St. Augustine's colonial archaeology goes online
item.description: The Florida Museum's iDigStAug portal opens St. Augustine archaeology to everyone, beginning with three colonial house sites and about 51,000 artifacts. Searchable records include finds, maps, photographs, field notes and freely available archival PDFs, with much more of the museum's million-object collection planned.

item.title: SPSFC 5 names its ten semifinalists
item.description: The fifth Self-Published Science Fiction Competition has advanced ten novels from its five judging teams. The slate ranges across technothrillers, first contact, space marines, virtual reality, time travel and generation ships, with links to each team's full announcement and every semifinalist book.

item.title: Mandrake's first two weeks reveal Lee Falk as artist
item.description: The Daily Cartoonist marks Mandrake the Magician's 1934 debut by reproducing much of the strip's first two weeks. The installment is especially useful because creator Lee Falk drew those opening strips himself before handing the artwork to Phil Davis, giving researchers a compact view of the feature's original form.

item.title: BlackRock marked down its Automattic investment again
item.description: BlackRock's March 2025 filing valued its Automattic shares at $31.03 each, down 17% from December and more than 25% year over year, according to The Repository. The markdown offers one of the few outside indicators of the private WordPress company's financial trajectory, though it does not disclose revenue or cash flow.

item.title: WordPress still powers about two-fifths of the web
item.description: An updated statistical roundup puts WordPress at 40.7% of all websites and 58.9% of sites using a known content-management system. It also inventories more than 71,000 free plugins and 30,000 themes. The figures are a useful snapshot of the platform's reach, although methodology and changing source data deserve scrutiny.

item.title: Authors Guild explains settlement disputes and rights reversions
item.description: The Authors Guild offers practical guidance for writers and publishers resolving allocation errors in Anthropic copyright-settlement claims. It explains how to update percentages, document reverted rights and use the 30-day dispute process, while warning claimants to avoid look-alike scam sites.

item.title: A practical guide to rebuilding old-school BBS door development
item.description: This hands-on introduction reconstructs development environments for BBS door programs on DOS, Windows, Linux and OS/2. It explains the old door kits, drop files, serial communications and carrier-loss handling, with links to period compilers and libraries for anyone reviving networked games from the dial-up era.

item.title: Criterion revisits the startling modernity of Quick Millions
item.description: A dispatch from Il Cinema Ritrovato argues that Rowland Brown's restored 1931 crime film Quick Millions rewrites the usual history of the gangster picture. Its cerebral amorality, flippant humor and offbeat style make the rise and fall of a ruthless trucker feel remarkably modern.
